name: The Brain
duty_cycle: Intermittent training, plus an hourly signal batch during market hours (cron fires :15 past every hour) that ADR-001 proposes moving off this machine

status.note: Operational. 49 signals published to date; the Gate-1 signal ledger went live 2026-08-30 and records one durable row per candidate at every gatekeeper exit. The material finding this week is that **the ML gatekeeper scores but does not gate**: it computes a real score for every live signal, but nothing compares that score to the champion's calibrated per-regime cutoff — `run.py` stamps a hardcoded 0.5, which is below all four of them. Measured 2026-08-30, applying the real cutoffs would refuse 14 of the 15 live map cells (~93%). The owner therefore declined activation and the gate runs in **shadow mode**: every ledger row carries what the gate *would* have decided, while live routing stays permissive and unchanged. Seven days of shadow data, then a decision. Heartbeat is WARN on `fact_trade_outcomes` staleness and 12-of-67 strategy instantiation failures — none of the 12 are in the live map.

summary.technical: System 1 is the offline intelligence factory. It ingests OANDA multi-timeframe candles, builds a versioned trailing-only feature store, fits causal regime labels, attributes historical trade outcomes to the regime in force at entry, vets each (strategy x regime x granularity) cell against fixed gates, trains an XGBoost gatekeeper on walk-forward folds, and publishes a checksummed artifact bundle. It never emits an order and holds no credential capable of placing one. It also currently runs a live signal producer — a contradiction that ADR-001 exists to resolve.
summary.plain: System 1 is the research lab. It reads years of price history, works out what kind of market each moment was, checks which trading rules actually made money in which kind of market, and packages the winners into a sealed box with a serial number on it. It never touches the money. Its job is to hand the box downstream and then be allowed to switch off.

facts.value: Hourly cron, fires :15 past every hour

facts.label: Queue transport
facts.value: Pub/Sub — publisher-only service account (can push, cannot list or pull)

technical: Ingestion is a single governed writer: `src/system1/ingestion/multi_timeframe_ingest.py`, fronted by `dq.py` data-quality gates. It pulls **MBA candles** (mid, bid and ask in one request) from the OANDA v20 REST practice endpoint across H1, H4 and D1, and writes to the `fact_market_prices` hypertable with `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (<pk>)` so a re-run is a no-op rather than a duplicate.

Every write goes through `src/common/db.py`. No module builds a connection string inline. Session timezone is pinned to UTC, because every day and week boundary in the risk layer downstream is computed in UTC and a local-time drift would silently move a daily loss budget.

Column casing is a real hazard in this schema: only `"Open"` and `"Close"` are mixed-case and `"timestamp"` is reserved, so all three are double-quoted; everything else is lowercase. Code is written schema-aware — optional columns are never assumed to exist, because the live schema has drifted from the original design.
plain: This step is the delivery bay. It phones the broker, asks for the price history of each currency pair at three different zoom levels — hourly, four-hourly and daily — and files it away.

Two things make it boring on purpose. First, asking twice does not create two copies; the second delivery is recognised and thrown away. Second, everything is stamped in one single timezone, so 'Tuesday' means the same Tuesday everywhere in the system.

callouts.title: The look-ahead trap this project actually fell into
callouts.technical: `detect_swing_points` used a centred rolling window (`center=True`), which reads bars *after* the one being labelled. It contaminated the only live strategy at the time and 36 of the 51 research strategies. Feature code is now required to pass `assert_no_lookahead_v2`.
callouts.plain: A helper function was quietly peeking at tomorrow's prices to decide what today looked like. Every result built on it was fiction — not wrong by a little, wrong in the way that makes a losing system look like a winning one. It is now checked automatically.

technical: The runtime is organised as tasks MODEL-001…010. Every module is a `python -m` entry point, separates pure math from I/O, and registers runs to MLflow. Walk-forward folds are shared from `validation/walk_forward.py` — min train 36 months, 6-month step, 6-month out-of-sample, anchored — so regimes, attribution and the gatekeeper all cut time the same way.

The controlling design decision is **strategy first, gatekeeper vetoes**. Strategies run blind on mechanical price rules with no idea what the regime is. The regime model labels history separately. Attribution joins the two *after the fact* at the trade's entry timestamp, using the causal label. This is what makes it possible to throw hundreds of dumb strategies at the wall without hand-coding regime logic into each one.

Promotion-capable stages default to dry-run. `vet` writes `results/reports/proposed_*` unless `--live`; `gatekeeper.train --dry-run` never touches the live champion. The orchestrator is the **single governed writer** of the champion bundle (FIX-S1-009) — a second promotion path is prohibited, not merely discouraged.
plain: Think of it as a hiring process for trading rules.

First, every candidate rule is let loose on decades of history with a blindfold on — it just follows its mechanical instructions and every trade it would have made is written down. Separately, a second program goes through the same history and marks each day with what the market was doing: trending, drifting sideways, or violent.

Then the two lists are laid on top of each other. Now you can ask a sharp question: *this rule made money — but was that in calm markets or wild ones?* Rules that only work in one kind of weather get used only in that weather.

Finally, a machine-learning referee learns to spot the trades that tend to fail even when the rule and the weather both look right, and gets a veto. Nothing is promoted automatically; almost every stage refuses to change anything unless explicitly told to.

stages.name: Multi-timeframe ingest
stages.technical: OANDA MBA candle fetch across H1/H4/D1 with data-quality gates on gaps, duplicates and stale bars.
stages.plain: Fetches the raw price history and refuses to accept it if there are holes in it.

stages.name: Feature pipeline
stages.technical: Versioned Parquet feature store. All features trailing-only, deterministic, byte-identical across runs.
stages.plain: Turns raw prices into the measurements the models actually read — trend strength, volatility, momentum.

stages.name: Regime detection
stages.technical: 4-state Gaussian HMM on D1/H4/H1 mapping to {Trending-Up, Trending-Down, Ranging, High-Vol}. K-Means fallback below the 0.70 accuracy gate. Emits a reporting label **and** a causal walk-forward label; only the causal one is allowed downstream.
stages.plain: Sorts market history into four kinds of weather. It produces two versions of the answer: a tidy hindsight one for charts, and a strict one that only used information available at the time. Only the strict one is allowed to influence money.

stages.name: Attribution
stages.technical: Point-in-time join of each trade to the causal regime at entry. Per (strategy x regime x granularity) metrics on **out-of-sample trades only**, with Bayesian shrinkage for thin cells.
stages.plain: Files each historical trade under the weather it was opened in, then scores each rule separately per weather type. Buckets with too few trades get their scores pulled toward the average — though as the gates section explains, that shrinkage is not currently enough to stop a five-trade cell qualifying.

stages.name: Vetting
stages.technical: Gates: PF ≥ 1.5, Sharpe ≥ 0.8, MaxDD ≤ 25%, WinRate ≥ 40%, Recovery ≥ 3.0, **OOS ≥ 12 months** — lowered from 60 by owner decision on 2026-08-21. `INTEGRITY_DISQUALIFIED` is checked **before** the performance gates, in a separate category. There is **no minimum trade-count gate**; `trade_count` is only a ranking tie-break.
stages.plain: The examiner. Six pass marks and a separate blacklist for rules whose past results are known to be fiction. One pass mark was deliberately relaxed in August, and there has never been a rule saying *how many trades* the evidence has to rest on — which is exactly how a five-trade track record ended up qualifying.

stages.name: Gatekeeper training
stages.technical: XGBoost on causal-regime features, expanding-window walk-forward, per-regime thresholds, bootstrap-significant OOS uplift required.
stages.plain: Trains the referee that can veto individual trades. It only counts as an improvement if the improvement survives a statistical shake-test.

stages.name: Serialize & publish
stages.technical: Immutable versioned prefixes, secret scan, SHA256 round-trip verify, then — and only then — an atomic `latest.json` pointer flip. Superseded pointer archived to `previous.json`; old versions are never overwritten.
stages.plain: Seals the box, re-checks the seal after shipping, and only then updates the sign that says 'this is the current box'. If the checks disagree, the shipment is deleted and the sign never moves.

stages.name: Signal producer
stages.technical: Schema-validated against `contracts/signal-message-contract.json`, idempotent by `message_id`, backpressure + DLQ. **The only online component in this repository** — and the subject of ADR-001, which proposes moving it to System 2 entirely.
stages.plain: Puts each scored trade idea in an envelope with a unique reference number and posts it. It is the only part of the research lab that has to be awake during market hours — which is precisely the problem an open architecture decision is trying to fix.

stages.name: Gate-1 signal ledger
stages.technical: One durable NDJSON row per trade candidate at **every** gatekeeper exit — scored, unscored, or dropped for a corrupt feature. The dropped case previously left a single log line with no `signal_id` and was unrecoverable once the log rotated. `fsync` per row, then a byte-offset delta upload to GCS on the same hourly cron, so a transport outage cannot touch emission. Each row pairs `model_score` with `threshold_calibrated` and a `shadow_verdict`, keyed on `regime_structural` — the label the model actually consumed, not the routing label — which is what makes the shadow rejection rate computable. It also records `gatekeeper_model_sha256` beside `bundle_id`, exposing per signal that the scoring model is not the published one.
stages.plain: A logbook for the referee. Every candidate it looks at gets exactly one line written down: what it scored, what the cut-off would have been, and whether the signal was sent on anyway. Because the referee's verdict is recorded but not acted on, we can measure exactly what switching it on would cost before switching it on.

stages.name: Retrain orchestrator
stages.technical: Triggers: Sunday 00:00 UTC, low Sharpe, circuit breaker. Single-flight lock, cooldown, gated pipeline, atomic promote only if gates pass **and** it beats the incumbent read from the storage backend (FIX-S1-007). The single governed writer of the champion bundle.
stages.plain: The foreman. Decides when a retrain is warranted, refuses to start a second one on top of a running one, and only replaces the current model if the new one is genuinely better than what is already deployed.

stages.name: Analytics bundle
stages.technical: Read-only downstream bundle: strategy catalog, per-trade OOS r-multiple series per qualified cell, frequency stats and regime occupancy. Same immutable-prefix + verify + pointer-flip-last contract. A failure here never affects the promote.
stages.plain: Publishes the supporting evidence so the other machines can show charts without needing access to this one's database. If it fails, the model still ships — it is a report, not a dependency.

callouts.title: The gates were relaxed, and one gate was never there
callouts.technical: On 2026-08-21 the owner lowered `oos_months` from 60 to 12. Separately, `vet.py` has never had a minimum trade-count gate — `trade_count` participates only as a ranking tie-break. The two together are why cells resting on 5, 13 and 20 out-of-sample trades now appear as `qualified` in the live map with profit factors of 6.8 to 13.6 and drawdowns of 0.02% to 1%.
callouts.plain: Two things happened. The owner deliberately shortened the minimum track record a strategy needs, from five years to one. And there has never been any rule about *how many* trades that track record must contain. Put together, a strategy with five trades in its history can now be waved through with a spectacular-looking score — and a five-trade score is noise, not skill.

callouts.title: The gatekeeper scores, but it does not gate
callouts.text: `Scorer.score()` returns `{status, score}` and never loads its own manifest, so the champion's calibrated per-regime cutoffs (High-Vol 0.80, Ranging 0.75, Trending-Down 0.60, Trending-Up 0.75) are never read at inference. The consumer stamps a hardcoded `threshold_applied = 0.5` — below every one of them — so every scored signal is published regardless of score, and the only true drop is a corrupt feature. A prior code comment claimed the gatekeeper could not score live at all; that described the previous champion and was retracted on 2026-08-30 after measurement showed 15 of 15 pair/granularity combinations scoring. Live scores cluster 0.42-0.46 against cutoffs of 0.60-0.80, so enforcing the gate today would refuse 14 of the 15 live map cells. That is the calibration working as designed — `shipped_approval_rate` is 0.079 — which is precisely why it is an owner decision about trading activity and not a bug fix. Tracked as FIX-S1-018.

technical: System 1 emits exactly two kinds of thing: **artifacts** to object storage and **messages** to a Pub/Sub topic. It never emits an order, and it holds no broker credential capable of placing one.

The publish contract is ordering-critical: upload to an immutable versioned prefix → SHA256 verify the round trip → only then flip `latest.json`. A consumer that reads the pointer therefore can never observe a half-written bundle. Retention trims the oldest versions; it never overwrites.

`QUEUE_PROVIDER` is now `pubsub` — it was `local` until recently, which meant signals landed in a directory on Computer 1 that no other machine could ever read. System 1's service account is **publisher-only**: it can push to `Scored_Signal_Queue` but cannot list topics or subscriptions, so it has no way to confirm anyone is on the other end.
plain: Two outputs, both one-way. A sealed model package on cloud storage, and a stream of scored trade ideas.
Nothing here can place a trade. That is deliberate — the machine that decides what is a good idea is physically incapable of acting on its own opinion.

The trade ideas now go into a real cloud postbox rather than a folder on one desk. But System 1 has posting rights only: it cannot look inside the postbox to check whether anyone is collecting. Confirmation has to come back from the other machines in writing.

callouts.title: The producer runs once a day, for strategies that trade six times a day
callouts.technical: The producer fires from `cron_daily_ingest_and_signals.sh` at 22:30, weekdays only. Two of the three live strategies are H4 — six bars per day — so a once-daily batch emits signals for bars that closed up to twenty hours earlier. `src/signals/run.py` already supports a continuous 60-second loop; the open decision is hourly cron versus continuous service, with hourly cron recommended as the smaller, restartable change.
callouts.plain: The trade ideas are posted once a night. But two of the three live strategies produce a new idea every four hours, so most of what gets posted is describing a moment that passed the previous afternoon. An idea that stale is not tradeable.

callouts.title: `wire_action: published` does not mean the broker saw it
callouts.text: The ledger row is written before publication. The producer then dead-letters individual messages after that point — BUILD_ERROR, SCHEMA_INVALID, BAD_REGIME, QUEUE_FULL, PUBLISH_NACK — and counts idempotent replays as deduped. So a `published` row with no matching `ams_decision_log` entry is either a lost message or a dead-letter. Under Pub/Sub `dead_letter()` publishes nothing to a DLQ topic, so those two are separated by the per-reason `dlq` counters in `s1_health.json` — a rate, never which row. It cannot support per-row wire-drop alerting.

sections.title: Running It — Logs, Health Checks & Commands

technical: System 1 has no dashboard of its own. Everything below is either a local file on Computer 1 or a single artifact mirrored to GCS that the other machines (and this documentation) can read without a database connection or SSH access.

Four cron jobs run the machine: an hourly job at **:15** (ingest → build/score/publish signals → publish health → mirror the model card), a legacy weekday-evening job at **22:30** that mostly duplicates the hourly one now, a daily heartbeat at **06:00**, and a Saturday catch-up ingest at **00:00**. The retrain cron is intentionally **not installed** — it is on a declared hold (`results/state/cron_holds.json`, expires 2026-09-15) at Computer 2's request.

The single most important state field in the whole system is `results/state/signal_emitter_state.json` → `last_signal_emitted_at`. It only advances on a real publish, never on a run — which is the direct fix for FIX-S1-016, where the producer ran on schedule for weeks, logged nothing alarming, and never once emitted a signal. A green heartbeat next to a null or stale `last_signal_emitted_at` is that failure mode recurring, not a healthy system.
plain: Nothing here needs a login or a dashboard. It's cron jobs writing plain files, plus one snapshot copied to the cloud so the other two computers can check on this one without asking it anything.

The one number that matters more than any other is the timestamp of the last signal actually sent — not the last time the job ran. A job can run perfectly, on schedule, forever, and still never send anything. That exact failure happened here once for weeks before anyone noticed, because everything that could be checked said 'healthy' except the one thing nobody was reading.

callouts.title: How to tell signals are actually running, not just that the cron fired
callouts.technical: Three checks, in order. (1) `crontab -l` — is the hourly job installed at all. (2) `signal_emitter_state.json` — is `last_run_at` within the last hour; if so, the process is alive. (3) `last_signal_emitted_at` — this is the field that can lie by omission if you only check (2). A live `last_run_at` next to a null or many-hours-stale `last_signal_emitted_at` is not necessarily broken by itself — see the next callout — but it is the exact shape FIX-S1-016 took, so it always deserves a second look, not an assumption.
callouts.plain: Three checks. Is the job even scheduled? Did it run in the last hour? And separately — did it actually *send* anything recently? The third question is the one that got missed for weeks before, because the first two can both be perfectly true while the third stays silent forever.

callouts.title: A quiet queue is not automatically a broken one
callouts.technical: The live strategies (`liquidity_grab_fade@H4`, `xard_ma_cross_daily_open@H1`, etc.) fire on a mechanical entry condition, not on a timer — roughly 3x/week/pair by design. A multi-hour gap between publishes during active market hours is normal variance, not evidence of failure. What *would* indicate a real problem: the hourly cron log shows `No signals generated` while a new closed bar was found (that's a routing or regime-coverage question, not a strategy-firing question), or `last_run_at` stops advancing altogether.
callouts.plain: These trading rules don't fire on a schedule — they fire when their specific pattern shows up in the price, which for the strategies currently live is roughly three times a week per currency pair. Going most of a day without a new signal is completely normal and not, by itself, something to worry about.

callouts.title: Cadence gap closed — the producer now runs hourly, not once a day
callouts.technical: Previously logged as GAP-S1-01: the producer fired once nightly at 22:30 while two of three live strategies were H4 (six bars/day), so signals could arrive up to 20 hours stale. `shell/cron_hourly_signals.sh` now runs at :15 past every hour; the cadence choice (hourly cron over a continuous service) was the smaller, more restartable change and matches the existing pattern. Verified against the live crontab and a week of `logs/cron_hourly_signals.log` (2026-08-24 through 2026-08-27): 24 runs/day, 46 real signals published across three trading days, zero dead-lettered.
callouts.plain: Trade ideas used to get posted once a night, which meant some of them described a market moment up to 20 hours old — too stale to be useful. They now get checked and posted every hour instead, confirmed by a full week of logs.

callouts.title: Resolved (badly) 2026-08-27 — the signals never arrived, and a real discrepancy remains open
callouts.technical: Superseding the note this callout originally carried. System 2/3's own trace of `ams_decision_log`, both services' logs and their write-ahead logs found: System 3's gate process (`ams.service.main`) and System 2's execution engine stopped simultaneously at 2026-08-24T17:07:53-55Z — no exception, no shutdown log line, no restart since. Separately, System 3 has never had a real Pub/Sub consumer: `pubsub_signal_relay.py` is meant to bridge `scored_signal_queue_sub` into its local queue but has no systemd unit and no log evidence it has ever run. `ams_decision_log` holds exactly one entry since 2026-08-23 (a Sunday drill signal) and zero for Mon/Tue/Wed — none of this week's 46 real signals reached System 3 at all. Zero OANDA fills, confirmed by System 2's own log as an operational gap, not a risk-gate rejection. That leaves a genuine, unresolved contradiction: this machine's own non-destructive Pub/Sub check (above) found the 46 real signals gone from `scored_signal_queue_sub`'s backlog, which should be impossible if nothing ever consumed them. Followed up 2026-08-27: the subscription's IAM policy grants `pubsub.subscriber` to exactly one identity, `trading-vm@scalable-brain.iam.gserviceaccount.com` (the shared VM System 2/3 run on) — so whatever drained it ran there, under that identity or a project-level role not visible in this binding. Cloud Audit Logs could settle it definitively but Data Access logging is not enabled for Pub/Sub in this project, so the exact caller and timestamp are not recoverable after the fact. Two pulls made from this machine this session, both without `--auto-ack`, returned the same single stray message each time — including the very first pull, before any action from here — which rules out this investigation as the cause. Leading hypothesis, unconfirmed: something on the shared VM (plausibly a manual or ad hoc run of the relay script, or a similar peek that auto-acked) drained the subscription without the messages ever reaching the decision pipeline. Recommend enabling Pub/Sub Data Access audit logs before this happens again.
callouts.plain: The optimistic read above was wrong, or at least incomplete. System 2 and System 3 checked their own records and found: their two main processes both stopped at the exact same second on Monday afternoon and never came back, and separately, the piece of software that's supposed to hand signals from the cloud queue to System 3 has no evidence it has ever actually run. Their decision log has nothing recorded for this whole week except one test signal from Sunday night. Zero trades happened — not because a risk check said no, but because nothing was there to even ask the question. What's still a real mystery: if nothing ever picked up those 46 signals, they should still be sitting in the queue, unread. They're not — something did take them off the queue. Nobody has found out what yet, and the logging needed to answer that definitively isn't turned on. Worth turning on before this happens again.

technical: As of 2026-08-27 the pipeline is functioning end to end, the producer runs hourly, and a model set is published and loading. The live `regime_strategy_map.json` was regenerated 2026-08-24 and now carries 15 (strategy x regime) entries across three regimes — considerably more than the 6-entry map recorded here previously, which predates that republish. The honest qualification stands regardless of count: most of these strategies qualified, or were designated in, on small out-of-sample samples under a gate the owner deliberately relaxed, and are running on a practice account as a stated, accepted risk rather than an established edge.
plain: Everything below is deliberately unflattering. The machinery works, and works more often now than it used to. What it has found so far still does not amount to proof that any of these strategies makes money.

callouts.title: Why 'honest zero' counted as progress
callouts.technical: Before 2026-08-14 the live map routed to `Range_Stochastic_Divergence`, whose attribution rows read PF 1.92 / Sharpe 1.07 — derived from outcomes produced by a look-ahead version of the strategy that emits zero signals when computed causally. Regenerating the map would not have removed it; a fresh `vet --live` would have re-qualified it. Only an integrity blocklist checked before the gates could.
callouts.plain: The system used to have exactly one strategy live, and its impressive track record was an illusion produced by a bug. Removing it dropped the measured value to zero — but it was always zero. The number became true, which is the only reason anything measured afterwards can be believed.

callouts.title: FIX-S1-016 — the producer had never emitted anything, ever
callouts.technical: Fixed and verified end to end on 2026-08-22. Two independent faults: it checked publication status on the wrong artifact, a condition nothing could ever satisfy; and it crashed on import because the causal routing label had been deleted along with a retired experiment. The bug survived for weeks precisely because trading depended on a machine nobody was watching — which is ADR-001's central argument.
callouts.plain: The component responsible for posting trade ideas had never successfully posted one in its entire life. It failed silently, on a computer that is usually asleep, so nothing looked broken. Both causes are now fixed and verified against the real cloud bundle.

issues.title: No minimum trade-count gate
issues.text: `vet.py` treats `trade_count` only as a ranking tie-break. Combined with the 2026-08-21 reduction of `oos_months` from 60 to 12, cells with 5, 13 and 20 trades reached the live map. Worth adding regardless of where the OOS threshold lands.

issues.title: Qualified strategies published with empty exits
issues.text: Map cells serialize with `exits: {}`. A strategy with no exit specification serializes cleanly and means nothing to whoever executes it. The map now carries 15 cells across 8 strategies — 12 `designated` (an owner override of a failed gate) and 3 `qualified` — so this affects considerably more than the three cells recorded when this gap was first written. Open defect in `vet.py`.

issues.title: Delivery is unverified past the first hop
issues.text: System 1's service account is publisher-only and cannot list topics or subscriptions. It can prove it published; it cannot see whether System 3 consumed, whether an order was sized, or whether System 2 filled anything. Partial, non-authoritative evidence gathered 2026-08-27 with a personal (non-service-account) gcloud identity: `scored_signal_queue_sub`'s backlog does not contain this week's 46 real signals, only one stray 2026-08-23 drill message — consistent with something consuming, not proof of a fill. Confirmation still has to arrive as a written reply from System 2/3 naming what actually happened to an approved order.

issues.title: Test fixtures leaked into the production queue artefact
issues.text: A test run once wrote fixtures into the live queue — the `entry: 1.05` messages System 2 observed. The leak path is not yet closed.

issues.title: RETRACTED — the outcomes writer is not destructive
issues.text: **This entry was wrong and is kept only so the correction is on the record.** It claimed `persist_trade_outcomes` did DELETE-then-rebuild with no transaction and that the default `--lookback-years 5` silently discarded half the history. Neither is true: the writer is `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` and never deletes, and the default is 10 years. Corrected 2026-08-29. The belief that the writer was dangerous to run is part of why it was only ever run by hand, and why the table went stale for thirteen days before it was given a cron.

issues.title: Finding A — weight starvation
issues.text: `gates.normalized_weights` shift-by-floor drives the lowest-scoring qualifier in a regime toward zero weight regardless of merit (Sharpe 1.74, PF 3.06 → weight 8e-8). Softmax or rank weighting proposed.

issues.title: `src/registry/` imports a removed package
issues.text: Retains imports of the deleted `regime_aware` package, gated behind the `regime_aware_port` universe. Latent — will not fire for the current three strategies.

issues.title: `layer2_config_adapter` emits T-SQL
issues.text: A leftover from the SQL Server era. Emits SQL that will not run against PostgreSQL. Reconcile or retire.

issues.title: T6 ATR case mismatch
issues.text: `engine_adapter` writes `df['atr']`, `StrategyBase` reads `df['ATR']`. Affects research verdicts only — the ten legacy strategies set uppercase themselves. Unfixed, no FIX doc.

issues.title: The gatekeeper does not gate — running in shadow
issues.text: Nothing at inference compares the model score to the champion's calibrated cutoff; `run.py` stamps a hardcoded 0.5, below all four. There is therefore no below-threshold refusal, and the runtime approval rate is undefined rather than zero. Scoring itself works — 15 of 15 pair/granularity combinations measured 2026-08-30. Enforcing the calibrated cutoffs today would refuse 14 of 15 live map cells (~93% fewer signals), so activation was declined and the gate records its verdict without acting on it. FIX-S1-018.

issues.title: The live scorer runs an unpublished champion
issues.text: `Scorer` loads a directory, not a pointer, so the model doing the scoring (`champion_model.pkl`, sha `23b6d4ca…`, written 2026-08-24 and never published) is not the artifact the wire names in `bundle_id` (`gk-d614163c`, sha `8845b442…`). The retrain that produced it did not promote — `oos_uplift_ok` failed — so this is drift, not a promotion. It compounds the shadow review: every `threshold_calibrated` and `shadow_verdict` is computed against a manifest nobody downstream can reproduce from the published bundle, so the review's own inputs are unverifiable until the model set is republished.

issues.title: The ledger does not record what was never built
issues.text: It records what the gatekeeper did to a fully-formed signal. `build_signals` discards candidates at roughly a dozen earlier points — no structural regime, no stop price, no take-profit, no ATR, an undecodable direction — all before `signal_id` is minted, so none of them leave a row. **Absence of a ledger row is not evidence a candidate never existed.** The no-ATR path is the one recorded as having once dropped 100% of signals silently.

issues.title: Remote ledger retention is stated but not enforced
issues.text: 365 days is declared for `telemetry/signals/` and there is no GCS lifecycle rule behind it; the `system1-rw` service account lacks even `storage.buckets.get`, so System 1 cannot set one. The local copy prunes at 90 days, after which the bucket is the sole archive. Any rule must be scoped to `telemetry/signals/` and nothing wider — `delete_prefix` is an undelimited prefix match, and `--lifecycle-file` replaces the whole config rather than appending to it.
